errors.quote: which agrees with the fact that the best pair (2.55, 33.5) has both larger
errors.problem: False. The best w (2.55) is larger than 2, but the best b (33.5) is smaller than 50. The negative slope for b at (2, 50) only says that raising b lowers the error near that point. It does not say which way the best b lies.
errors.fix: Say that the best pair has a larger w but a smaller b. Explain that the slopes only give the downhill direction at the current point: early steps raise b because w is still too small, and later steps bring b down to 33.5 as w approaches 2.55. Each step is local, so the direction is recomputed every time.

errors.problem: The stated output cannot be right. The filter keeps only names that end with "_", and '_residues' starts with an underscore but does not end with one, so it can never be in this list in any version. The hedge about versions does not cover this. The claim that follows, "every attribute created by fit ends in an underscore", is also false: fit can also create private attributes whose names start with an underscore (as '_residues' itself shows), and this filter hides them.
errors.fix: Remove '_residues' from the output, e.g. ['n_features_in_', 'coef_', 'rank_', 'singular_', 'intercept_'], and keep the hedge about versions. Replace the claim with: the public attributes that fit estimates end in an underscore, and private names that start with an underscore are internal and not meant to be used.

errors.quote: This "numbers replace the data" picture is exact for linear regression only
errors.problem: Wrong note. A fixed set of fitted numbers replaces the training data in many other models too, for example logistic regression, linear SVMs and neural networks. Even a decision tree keeps only its thresholds and leaf values, not the rows. k-nearest neighbours is the real exception. The lesson body has a milder version of the same overreach: "Other models work differently."
errors.fix: Change the note to: this picture is exact for linear regression and for other models with a fixed set of fitted parameters (e.g. logistic regression). k-nearest neighbours is different because it keeps the training rows, and a tree stores thresholds rather than weights. In the body, write "Some models work differently".

errors.quote: A straight line through only two rows always has zero error.
errors.problem: Stated as absolute but only true when the two rows have different sizes. Two houses with the same size and different prices cannot both lie on one line.
errors.fix: Write "through two rows with different sizes always has zero error".

improvements.quote: **Hyperparameters** are settings a person chooses before fitting
improvements.problem: scikit-learn's own documentation uses "parameters" for the constructor settings (the "Parameters" section of every class page, get_params(), set_params()). It calls the fitted values such as coef_ and intercept_ "attributes". The learner will read those pages right away and find the lesson's key word used for the opposite thing. The extension also calls every constructor argument a hyperparameter, but copy_X and n_jobs do not change the fitted model at all.
improvements.fix: Add one or two sentences: in scikit-learn's docs, the settings you pass to LinearRegression(...) are listed under "Parameters" (that is, hyperparameters in this lesson's sense), and the fitted numbers are listed under "Attributes"; you can see both with model.get_params() and with coef_/intercept_. In the extension, say that some constructor arguments, such as copy_X and n_jobs, only control how the computation runs and are not modelling choices.

improvements.quote: and no pair of numbers does better on these four rows
improvements.problem: The learner tries three pairs and is then told that the third is the best of all possible pairs. Section 5 gives the formula but not why it gives the minimum, so the central idea ('fitting = smallest error') ends up taken on trust, which is what the plan wanted to avoid.
improvements.fix: Add a short check with the existing mean_squared_error: nudging each number in either direction raises the error. (2.55, 32.5) and (2.55, 34.5) both give 18.5, and (2.54, 33.5) and (2.56, 33.5) both give 18.19, against 17.5 at the best pair. Point out the two facts that mark the minimum: the errors 1, 2, -7, 4 sum to 0, and the sum of error × size, 50 + 140 - 630 + 440, is also 0. These are the two conditions the closed form solves, and they link straight to the gradient extension.

improvements.quote: Other models find their parameters by searching step by step (see below).
improvements.problem: Too broad (honest scope), and repeated in the notes. Linear regression with many features and ridge regression also have direct least-squares solutions. Decision trees are built by greedy splitting, not by gradually nudging numbers, and k-nearest neighbours does no search at all. Step-by-step gradient-based search is typical of models such as logistic regression and neural networks.
improvements.fix: Say that many models, such as logistic regression and neural networks, have no closed form and find their parameters step by step. Note that linear regression with several features is still solved directly, and that trees and k-NN fit in other ways. Change the note to match.

improvements.quote: Repeating the update many times walks the pair toward the smallest error.
improvements.problem: The extension describes gradient descent but gives the learner nothing to run or observe, so it reads more as a description than something the learner could rebuild. It also hides a real effect the learner will hit when trying it: with step 0.0001, b moves only about 0.0055 per step while w moves fast, because sizes are around 100 and b's input is 1. Reaching (2.55, 33.5) takes hundreds of thousands of steps, and a step above about 0.000145 makes it diverge.
improvements.fix: Add a short loop that computes the two numbers from the errors, updates w and b, and prints them every 50,000 steps. Also give a check of the gradient formula itself: mean_squared_error(2.001, 50) is about 920.06, a drop of about 4.94 for a 0.001 change in w, which matches -4950 per unit. Say plainly that convergence is slow here because the feature is not scaled, and that centring or scaling the sizes (a later topic) is the usual fix.
